Every citizen of the Union has the right to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States, but under the 2004 Citizens' Rights Directive that right is graded according to the length of stay. For up to three months, a citizen needs nothing more than a valid identity card or passport. Beyond three months, the right of residence depends on the person's situation: workers and self-employed people qualify, while students and economically inactive people must have sufficient resources not to become a burden on the host state's social assistance system, as well as comprehensive sickness insurance. Host states may require registration with the authorities after three months.

After five years of continuous legal residence, a citizen acquires the right of permanent residence, which is no longer subject to these conditions. It is lost only through absence from the host state for more than two consecutive years. Family members, including those who are not themselves EU citizens, enjoy rights derived from the citizen's.

Protection against expulsion also increases over time. A host state may restrict free movement on grounds of public policy, public security or public health, but such measures must be proportionate and based exclusively on the personal conduct of the individual concerned. Once a citizen has resided in the host state for the previous ten years, expulsion is possible only on imperative grounds of public security.

Being an EU citizen brings a practical advantage when travelling outside the Union. If a citizen is in a country where their own Member State has no embassy or consulate able to help, they are entitled to the protection of the diplomatic or consular authorities of any other Member State, on the same conditions as that state's own nationals. The right is set out in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and repeated in the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and a 2015 directive lays down how it is to be applied.

The assistance covers situations such as arrest or detention, being the victim of a crime, a serious accident or illness, and death, as well as relief and repatriation in an emergency. It can include issuing an emergency travel document to a citizen whose passport has been lost or stolen. The directive also sets out how Member States should cooperate during crises, for example when large numbers of citizens must be evacuated from a conflict zone, with EU Delegations helping to coordinate.

The assisting state may ask the citizen's own Member State to reimburse the costs it incurs, and the citizen can in turn be asked to repay them. The right applies to unrepresented citizens: a traveller whose own country has an embassy able to help must turn to it.

The European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, based in Vienna, was established in 2007. It replaced the European Monitoring Centre on Racism and Xenophobia, which had been set up a decade earlier, and its broader remit reflects a shift from a focus on racism to fundamental rights as a whole. Its task is to provide the EU institutions and the Member States with independent, evidence-based advice when they act within the scope of EU law.

Much of the agency's work consists of research. Its large-scale surveys, which ask thousands of people across the Union about their experiences, have covered subjects such as violence against women, antisemitism, and the situation of LGBTIQ people, Roma and migrants. Because comparable official statistics are often lacking, these surveys are frequently the main EU-wide source on such questions, and policymakers have drawn on their findings. The agency also issues opinions on draft legislation at the request of the institutions.

There are important limits to its role, however. The agency cannot examine individual complaints, and it has no power to take legal action against Member States or to impose sanctions. Nor does it decide whether there is a risk of a serious breach of the Union's values: that decision belongs to the institutions under Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union.

When the European Commission considers that a Member State has failed to fulfil an obligation under EU law, for example by not transposing a directive on time or by applying it incorrectly, it can open an infringement procedure under Article 258 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The procedure begins with a letter of formal notice asking the government for its observations. If the reply is unsatisfactory, the Commission sends a reasoned opinion explaining why it believes EU law is being breached and setting a deadline for compliance. Only if the Member State still does not comply may the Commission refer the case to the Court of Justice. Most cases are closed long before that stage.

A judgment finding an infringement is declaratory: the Court establishes that an obligation has been breached, and the Member State must take the necessary measures. If it fails to do so, the Commission can bring the case back to the Court under Article 260, which may then impose a lump sum, a periodic penalty payment, or both. Since the Treaty of Lisbon, however, where a Member State has failed to notify measures transposing a directive, the Commission may ask the Court to impose financial penalties in the first judgment.

The Commission enjoys broad discretion over whether and when to open a case, and individuals who complain to it cannot compel it to act.

Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union provides a procedure for cases in which a Member State threatens the values on which the Union is founded, such as democracy, the rule of law and respect for human rights. It has two distinct stages. Under the preventive arm, the Council, acting by a majority of four fifths of its members after obtaining the consent of the European Parliament, may determine that there is a clear risk of a serious breach of those values. Such a proposal may come from one third of the Member States, from the Parliament or from the Commission.

The sanctioning arm goes further. The European Council, acting unanimously on a proposal from one third of the Member States or from the Commission, and again with the Parliament's consent, may determine the existence of a serious and persistent breach. The Member State concerned does not take part in the vote. Only after such a determination may the Council, by qualified majority, suspend certain of that state's rights, including its voting rights in the Council.

The preventive arm has been triggered twice: by the Commission against Poland in 2017 and by the Parliament against Hungary in 2018. Neither case has led to a determination by the Council, and the procedure concerning Poland was closed in 2024 after the Commission withdrew its proposal. Many observers attribute the procedure's limited impact to the unanimity required at the second stage.

Since 1 January 2021, the EU has had a general regime of conditionality to protect its budget. Under the regulation, the Council can adopt measures such as suspending payments or commitments when breaches of the principles of the rule of law in a Member State affect, or seriously risk affecting, the sound financial management of the EU budget or the protection of the Union's financial interests in a sufficiently direct way. Breaches of the rule of law that have no such link with the budget fall outside its scope; they are dealt with by other instruments.

The procedure is started by the Commission, which must first notify the Member State and give it an opportunity to respond. The Council then decides on a Commission proposal by qualified majority, so no single government can block a decision. Measures must be proportionate, and they can be lifted if the situation is remedied. Importantly, the government concerned remains obliged to make payments to the final recipients and beneficiaries of EU programmes, such as students or farmers, so that they do not bear the consequences.

Hungary and Poland challenged the regulation before the Court of Justice, which dismissed both actions in February 2022. In December 2022, the Council used the mechanism for the first time, suspending about €6.3 billion in commitments under three cohesion programmes for Hungary.

Mutual recognition, described by EU leaders at the Tampere European Council in 1999 as the cornerstone of judicial cooperation, means that a decision taken by a judicial authority in one Member State is recognised and executed in another with a minimum of formalities, rather than being re-examined from scratch. The idea rests on mutual trust that each Member State's justice system offers adequate safeguards.

The European Investigation Order applies this principle to evidence. Since 2017, an authority investigating a crime in one of the participating Member States can issue an order asking another to carry out investigative measures, such as hearing witnesses, searching premises or obtaining banking information, and to transfer the evidence obtained. The executing authority must decide whether to recognise the order within 30 days and, in principle, carry out the measure within 90 days of that decision. It may refuse only on grounds listed in the directive, for example where execution would be incompatible with fundamental rights obligations, and it may in some cases use a different, less intrusive measure if that would achieve the same result.

Mutual trust is not blind trust, however. Critics point out that procedural safeguards still differ between Member States, and some commentators argue that the system serves prosecutors better than defendants, who have fewer practical means of gathering evidence abroad.

Between 2010 and 2016, the EU adopted six directives setting common minimum standards for the rights of suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings. The reasoning was that judges would find it easier to trust decisions taken elsewhere in the Union if they could rely on a common floor of procedural guarantees. The directives cover the right to interpretation and translation, the right to information, the right of access to a lawyer, the presumption of innocence and the right to be present at trial, special safeguards for children, and legal aid.

The directive on the right to information requires that people who are arrested be given promptly a written 'letter of rights' in a language they understand, explaining, for example, their right to remain silent and their right of access to a lawyer. The directive on the presumption of innocence prohibits public authorities from referring to suspects as guilty before a final conviction, and it states that the burden of proof lies with the prosecution.

The directives lay down minimum standards only, and Member States are free to provide a higher level of protection. Implementation has nevertheless been uneven, and the Commission has opened infringement procedures against several Member States for failing to transpose some of the directives correctly or on time.

EU anti-discrimination law rests largely on two directives adopted in 2000. The Racial Equality Directive prohibits discrimination on grounds of racial or ethnic origin not only in employment but also in social protection, including social security and healthcare, in education, and in access to goods and services available to the public, including housing. The Employment Equality Directive covers discrimination based on religion or belief, disability, age and sexual orientation, but only in employment, occupation and vocational training. Discrimination on grounds of sex is addressed by separate gender equality directives.

The resulting protection is uneven. A person refused a flat because of their ethnic origin can rely on EU law, whereas a person refused the same flat because of their age or sexual orientation cannot, unless national law provides protection, as it does in many Member States. A Commission proposal of 2008 to extend protection beyond employment for these other grounds did not obtain the unanimity required in the Council.

Both directives shift the burden of proof. Once a complainant establishes facts from which it may be presumed that there has been discrimination, it is for the respondent to prove that the principle of equal treatment has not been breached. Both also require Member States to ensure that victims have access to judicial or administrative procedures and that sanctions are effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

In The Logic of Scientific Discovery, first published in German in 1934, Karl Popper proposed a criterion for distinguishing science from non-science. A theory is scientific, he argued, not because it has been confirmed many times but because it is falsifiable: it rules out certain observable outcomes and could therefore be shown to be false. Popper stressed a logical asymmetry. No finite number of observations can prove a universal statement such as 'all swans are white', whereas a single well-established black swan refutes it. Science, on this view, advances through bold conjectures and attempts at refutation rather than by piling up confirmations.

Popper used the criterion to criticise theories that he believed could accommodate any outcome, citing certain versions of psychoanalysis and of Marxist history. A theory that explains everything, he argued, explains nothing.

Critics pointed to complications. Scientists never test a hypothesis in isolation: every prediction also relies on auxiliary assumptions about instruments, initial conditions and background theories. When a prediction fails, it is therefore logically open to blame one of these assumptions rather than the main theory. Historians of science such as Thomas Kuhn added that scientists often keep a successful theory despite anomalies, and that this tenacity has sometimes been productive. Popper accepted that falsification in practice is never conclusive, but he maintained that methodological rules should prevent theories from being rescued by ad hoc adjustments.

Kuhn argued that keeping a theory in spite of anomalies has always proved to be productive.

In 2015, a large collaboration of researchers published in the journal Science the results of an attempt to repeat 100 experiments that had appeared in three leading psychology journals. Whereas 97 of the original studies had reported statistically significant results, only about 36% of the replications did, and the effects found in the replications were on average about half the size of the original ones. The project did not show that the original findings were wrong: a single failed replication can itself be a false negative, and some replications differed from the originals in their samples or procedures.

Nevertheless, the results, together with similar projects in economics and cancer biology, fuelled a debate about a 'replication crisis'. Several causes have been proposed. Journals have tended to favour novel and positive findings, so studies with null results often remain unpublished. Small samples make estimates unstable. Researchers can also, often without any intention to deceive, try several analyses and report the one that crosses the threshold of statistical significance, a practice known as p-hacking.

Reforms have followed. In preregistration, researchers publicly record their hypotheses and analysis plan before collecting data. Some journals now offer 'registered reports', accepting a study for publication on the basis of its design, before the results are known. Supporters argue that these measures reduce bias, while sceptics worry that they may discourage exploratory research.

Magna Carta was agreed by King John of England at Runnymede in June 1215, under pressure from rebellious barons. It was a practical peace settlement rather than a statement of universal principles: most of its clauses dealt with specific grievances about feudal payments, inheritance, royal forests and the administration of justice. As a peace settlement it failed almost at once. John asked Pope Innocent III to annul it, the Pope declared it null and void in August 1215, and civil war resumed.

The charter nevertheless survived. After John's death in 1216, the regents governing for his young son Henry III reissued it in revised form, and further versions followed in 1217 and 1225. The 1225 version, granted in exchange for a tax, became the definitive text and was confirmed many times by later kings.

Its lasting fame rests on a few clauses, above all the promise that no free man would be imprisoned or deprived of his property except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land. In the seventeenth century, opponents of royal power reinterpreted this promise as a guarantee of fundamental liberties, and the charter later influenced constitutional thinking in the American colonies. Today only three of its clauses remain part of the law of England and Wales.

In The Rules of Sociological Method, published in 1895, Émile Durkheim made a claim that many readers found shocking: crime is a normal feature of society. He did not mean that crime is desirable or that it should go unpunished. His point was partly statistical. Crime is found in societies of every type, so a society entirely without it would be the abnormal case. A rate of crime far above what is usual for a given type of society would, in his view, be pathological.

Durkheim argued that crime also performs functions. When a rule is broken and the offender is punished, members of the community are reminded of the norms they share, and their collective sentiments are reinforced. Crime may also prepare change: by showing that existing norms can be challenged, it leaves room for moral evolution. His example was Socrates, condemned as a criminal under Athenian law, whose independence of thought helped prepare a new morality.

Durkheim illustrated the inevitability of deviance with an imaginary community of saints in an exemplary monastery. There, he suggested, crimes in the ordinary sense would be unknown, but faults that seem venial to ordinary people would cause the same scandal that ordinary offences cause elsewhere. What counts as crime, in other words, depends on the strength of collective sentiments, not on a fixed list of acts.

Durkheim argued that every crime contributes to the moral evolution of the society concerned.

In A Theory of Justice, published in 1971, John Rawls asked which principles of justice free and rational people would choose if they did not know what position they would occupy in society. Behind this 'veil of ignorance', the parties do not know their class, social status, natural talents, conception of the good life or even the generation to which they belong. Because no one can tailor the principles to their own advantage, Rawls argued, the choice would be fair, and he called his theory 'justice as fairness'.

He claimed that the parties would choose two principles. The first gives each person an equal right to the most extensive system of basic liberties compatible with a similar system for all. The second allows social and economic inequalities only if they are attached to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity and are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society, a condition known as the difference principle. The first principle has priority: basic liberties may not be traded for economic gains.

The theory has been both influential and widely criticised. Robert Nozick argued that it ignores how holdings were acquired and fails to respect people's rights over the fruits of their work. Others have questioned whether the parties would really be as cautious as Rawls assumed, since a willingness to gamble could lead them to prefer arrangements that maximise average welfare.

Article 107 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union declares support granted by a Member State, or through state resources, incompatible with the internal market when it distorts or threatens to distort competition by favouring certain undertakings, in so far as it affects trade between Member States. The prohibition is not absolute. The Treaty itself lists categories that are or may be compatible, such as aid to promote the development of areas where the standard of living is abnormally low or to remedy a serious disturbance in the economy of a Member State.

As a rule, governments must notify planned aid to the European Commission and may not put it into effect until the Commission has approved it. Many measures, however, escape this obligation. The General Block Exemption Regulation allows certain categories, for example some aid for research, training or environmental protection, to be granted without prior notification provided that its conditions are met, and small amounts fall outside the rules altogether: since 2024 the de minimis ceiling has been €300,000 per undertaking over three years.

Aid that should have been notified but was paid without approval is unlawful. If the Commission then finds it incompatible, it orders the Member State to recover it from the beneficiary, with interest. The aim is to restore the situation that existed before the aid was granted, not to punish the company, but recovery can still threaten the survival of a firm that has already spent the money.

Under the EU Merger Regulation, concentrations with an 'EU dimension' must be notified to the European Commission and may not be completed until they have been cleared. Whether a deal has an EU dimension depends on turnover: in the main test, the companies concerned must have a combined worldwide turnover above €5 billion, and at least two of them must each have turnover above €250 million in the EU. Even then, the deal is left to national authorities if each company achieves more than two-thirds of its EU turnover in one and the same Member State. This 'one-stop shop' spares merging firms from filing in several countries at once.

The Commission assesses whether a deal would significantly impede effective competition, in particular by creating or strengthening a dominant position. Most notified mergers are cleared in a first phase of 25 working days, many of them under a simplified procedure. Where serious doubts remain, the Commission opens an in-depth second phase, which normally lasts 90 working days and can be extended.

Outright prohibitions are rare. More often, the parties offer remedies, such as selling a business or licensing technology, to address the Commission's concerns, and the deal is approved subject to those commitments. Critics argue that the rules can prevent the creation of European champions able to compete globally, while supporters reply that consumers benefit from competition at home.

Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union prohibits agreements between companies that restrict competition, and cartels, in which competitors secretly fix prices, share markets or limit output, are among the most serious forms. When the European Commission finds an infringement, it can impose a fine of up to 10% of a company's total worldwide turnover in the preceding business year. Within that ceiling, the amount depends on the value of the sales concerned, the gravity of the infringement and its duration, and it can be increased for repeat offenders.

Because cartels are secret, the Commission relies heavily on its leniency programme. The first company to report a cartel and provide evidence that enables the Commission to carry out an inspection or find an infringement may receive full immunity from fines. Companies that come forward later can obtain reductions if they supply evidence of significant added value: 30 to 50% for the first of them, 20 to 30% for the next and up to 20% for any others. Separately, firms that acknowledge their participation can settle the case and receive a further 10% reduction.

Leniency does not protect a company from everything. Victims of a cartel can sue its members for damages before national courts, although a firm that received immunity is generally liable only towards its own direct and indirect purchasers or providers.

The Digital Markets Act, which became applicable in May 2023, targets a small number of large online platforms that act as 'gatekeepers' between businesses and consumers. A company is presumed to be a gatekeeper if it provides a core platform service, such as an online search engine, an app store or a messaging service, in at least three Member States and meets thresholds based on its size and reach: an annual EU turnover of at least €7.5 billion in each of the last three years or a market value of at least €75 billion, together with at least 45 million monthly active end users and 10,000 yearly active business users in the EU. Firms meeting the thresholds must notify the Commission, which then designates them; a company may put forward arguments to rebut the presumption, but the Commission decides.

Unlike traditional competition law, which intervenes after harm has been shown, the Act lays down obligations in advance. Gatekeepers may not, for instance, rank their own products more favourably than those of rivals, and they must allow users to uninstall pre-installed apps.

Breaches can lead to fines of up to 10% of worldwide turnover, rising to 20% for repeated infringements. In September 2023 the Commission designated six gatekeepers, and the online travel platform Booking was added in 2024.

Value added tax (VAT) is charged at each stage of production and distribution, but businesses can deduct the VAT they pay on their purchases from the VAT they charge on their sales. As a result, the tax is in principle borne by the final consumer, while businesses act as collectors for the state. The EU's VAT Directive sets common rules, yet Member States still choose their own rates within limits: the standard rate must be at least 15%, and reduced rates, which may apply only to goods and services listed in the Directive, may not normally fall below 5%. A reform adopted in 2022 gave governments more flexibility, including the possibility of a zero rate for a limited number of essential items.

For online sales to consumers in other Member States, VAT is in general due in the country where the goods are delivered. Since July 2021, sellers have been able to declare and pay this VAT through a single online portal, the One-Stop Shop, in their own country instead of registering in each Member State of their customers. Small sellers whose cross-border sales to consumers stay below €10,000 a year may instead apply the VAT of their home country.

Despite these rules, the gap between the VAT that should be collected and what is actually received remains large, partly because of fraud schemes that exploit the exemption for goods moving between Member States.

The Services Directive, adopted in 2006, was designed to make it easier for businesses to set up in another Member State or to provide services there temporarily without settling. Services account for most of the EU's economic activity, yet cross-border trade in services has long lagged behind trade in goods, partly because of national rules on authorisations, legal form and professional qualifications.

The Directive requires Member States to simplify their procedures and to provide 'points of single contact', through which providers can complete the necessary formalities online. When a provider from another Member State offers services temporarily, any national requirement imposed on it must be non-discriminatory, justified by reasons of public policy, public security, public health or protection of the environment, and proportionate. Certain requirements, such as conditions based on nationality, are banned outright.

The Directive does not cover every service. Financial services, healthcare, transport, audiovisual services, gambling and services provided by temporary work agencies, among others, are excluded or governed by their own rules. The original proposal would have subjected providers working across borders mainly to the rules of their home country. Posting is distinct from free movement of workers, where a person moves to another country to take up a job there. The Posting of Workers Directive, first adopted in 1996, guarantees posted workers a core set of the host country's terms and conditions, including maximum work periods, minimum paid annual leave and health and safety rules.

A revision that has applied since July 2020 strengthened the principle of equal pay for equal work at the same place. Posted workers are now entitled to the host country's remuneration as set by law or by universally applicable collective agreements, not merely its minimum wage, and reimbursements for travel, board and lodging cannot be counted towards that pay. Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union prohibits the abuse of a dominant position. Being dominant is not unlawful in itself: a company may win a large market share by offering better or cheaper products, and competition law does not aim to protect less efficient rivals from that. What is prohibited is conduct by which a dominant firm exploits customers or excludes competitors by means other than competition on the merits, for example by charging unfair prices, tying one product to another or granting rebates on condition that customers buy all or most of their needs from it.

Dominance is assessed in a defined market. A market share above 50% is generally treated as a strong indication of it, although lower shares can be enough in some circumstances. In recent decades the Commission and the EU courts have placed greater weight on the actual or likely effects of conduct, rather than on its form alone.

The Google Shopping case shows how these rules apply to digital markets. In 2017 the Commission fined Google €2.42 billion for favouring its own comparison shopping service in its general search results while demoting rival services. Google challenged the decision before the EU courts, but in 2024 the Court of Justice upheld it, confirming that a dominant platform can abuse its position by treating its own services more favourably than those of competitors.

Owners of good cars then find that price too low and keep their cars off the market, which lowers the average quality on offer, and with it the price buyers will pay. Studies of firms in the United States around the year 2000 found that when they switched to automatic enrolment, with the possibility to opt out, participation among new employees rose sharply, even though the financial incentives were unchanged. Researchers suggest several reasons: inertia and procrastination, the effort of comparing options, and the sense that the default carries an implicit recommendation from the employer. In a widely cited article published in 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin described what he called the 'tragedy of the commons'. Imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding another animal, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone. Acting rationally, each keeps adding animals until the pasture is ruined. Hardin concluded that shared resources would be destroyed unless they were either privatised or controlled by the state.

The political scientist Elinor Ostrom challenged this conclusion. Studying fisheries, forests, irrigation systems and mountain pastures around the world, including communities in Switzerland and Japan that had managed common land for centuries, she found that users were often able to manage a common resource sustainably without either privatisation or central control. Successful arrangements tended to share certain features: clear boundaries defining who may use the resource, rules adapted to local conditions, monitoring by people accountable to the users, graduated sanctions for those who break the rules and cheap ways of resolving conflicts.

Ostrom did not claim that communities always succeed; she documented many failures too, particularly where users could not communicate or where outsiders could easily take the resource. In 2009 she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, which she shared with Oliver Williamson.

The term 'Dutch disease' was coined by The Economist magazine in 1977 to describe the problems that followed the discovery of a large natural gas field in the Netherlands in 1959. As gas exports grew, the Dutch currency strengthened, and manufacturing firms found it harder to sell their goods abroad. Unemployment rose even though the country was earning substantial revenue from gas.

Economists have since used the term for a wider pattern. When a country starts exporting large amounts of a natural resource, the inflow of foreign currency tends to push up its exchange rate. Other export sectors, such as manufacturing or agriculture, become less competitive, and labour and capital may move towards the booming resource sector and towards services that cannot be traded across borders, such as construction. If the resource later runs out or its price falls, the economy may be left with a weakened industrial base that is slow to recover.

The effect is not inevitable. Norway, which began producing oil in the early 1970s, places its revenue from oil and gas in a sovereign wealth fund that invests abroad, and the government limits how much of the fund it spends each year. Investing the revenue outside the country reduces the upward pressure on the currency and spreads the benefits across generations.

All phones sold in the EU from February 2027 must have batteries that their owners can remove and replace.

Because the regulation is aimed at imports, wood harvested in the forests of EU Member States falls outside the scope of its rules.

Any Member State may decide to delay meeting the new limit values until 2040 if it finds them too costly.
Most cities in the EU already comply with the limit for fine particulate matter that applies from 2030.
The new EU annual limit for nitrogen dioxide is double the value recommended by the WHO.

Adopted in 1991, the Nitrates Directive aims to protect waters from pollution caused by nitrates from agricultural sources, mainly fertilisers and livestock manure. In vulnerable zones, farmers must follow action programmes that include periods when spreading fertiliser is prohibited, rules on storing manure and a limit on the quantity of nitrogen from livestock manure that can be applied: 170 kilograms per hectare per year.

The Commission may grant derogations allowing higher amounts in specific conditions, for instance on farms with a long growing season and crops that take up a lot of nitrogen, such as grassland. Member States must report on water quality every four years, and the Commission has repeatedly taken countries to court over insufficient designation or weak action programmes.

A Member State may apply action programmes throughout its territory rather than designating particular zones.
Nitrate pollution from agriculture in the EU has fallen steadily since the directive was adopted in 1991.
The 50 mg/l threshold was chosen because higher nitrate levels in drinking water are dangerous for infants.

The regulation contains no restoration targets for urban areas or rivers, which are left to the Member States.
All of the regulation's targets can be suspended for a time if exceptional events threaten food production.

That changed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when supply cuts and price spikes exposed the risk of entering the cold months with low stocks. Countries with large storage capacity relative to their consumption did not have to fill beyond a volume equal to 35% of their average annual gas consumption over the previous five years. Member States without storage facilities on their territory had to ensure that the equivalent of 15% of their annual consumption was held in storage in other Member States, or contribute to the effort in another agreed way.

The rules were initially due to expire at the end of 2025. In 2025 they were extended until the end of 2027, but with more flexibility over the timing and level of filling, after traders and some governments complained that a rigid deadline pushed up summer prices by signalling to the market exactly when large volumes had to be bought.

The filling rules were the main reason why European wholesale gas prices fell in the years following 2022.
Under the 2022 rules, not every Member State with storage facilities had to fill them to 90% of their capacity.
The EU met its storage filling target each year from 2022 to 2025, despite the loss of most Russian gas supplies.

European airspace has traditionally been organised along national borders, with each country responsible for air traffic control over its own territory. As a result, flights often follow routes that are longer than necessary, and controllers in neighbouring centres use systems that are not always compatible. The initiative rests on several instruments. A performance scheme sets targets for air navigation service providers in areas such as delays, cost-efficiency and flight efficiency. A Network Manager, a role entrusted to Eurocontrol, coordinates route design and traffic flows across Europe. SESAR, the technological pillar, develops and deploys new air traffic management systems.

Progress has been slower than its supporters hoped. Member States regard airspace as closely linked to national sovereignty and defence, and military needs restrict how some areas can be used. Functional airspace blocks, intended to merge the management of airspace across borders, largely failed to deliver the expected integration. A reform agreed in 2024 updated the framework, but airlines argue that air traffic control strikes and staff shortages in some countries remain a major cause of delays.

options: Functional airspace blocks achieved none of the cross-border integration that they were designed to deliver.
Shortening the routes that flights follow is one way in which the initiative is meant to reduce emissions.
SESAR is run as a public-private partnership bringing together the EU, Eurocontrol and the aviation industry.
Airlines blame air traffic control strikes for most of the flight delays recorded in European airspace.

Criteria are set for product groups such as cleaning products, paints, textiles and tourist accommodation, and they take account of a product's environmental impact throughout its life cycle, from raw materials to disposal. Applications are assessed by competent bodies in each Member State, and compliance is checked by an independent party rather than simply declared by the producer. A directive adopted in 2024 to empower consumers for the green transition addresses this problem. From 27 September 2026, traders may no longer make generic environmental claims, such as 'eco-friendly', when they cannot demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance. Nor may they display sustainability labels that are not based on a certification scheme or established by public authorities. Labels such as the EU Ecolabel are therefore unaffected by this ban, while some retailers' own logos may have to be withdrawn or redesigned.

Since late 2026, all environmental claims on products are banned unless they are backed by the EU Ecolabel.
Products carrying the EU Ecolabel sell better than comparable products that do not carry the label.
Wine is never eligible for the EU Ecolabel, however sustainably the grapes are grown.

The EU's Waste Framework Directive ranks ways of dealing with waste in a 'waste hierarchy'. Prevention comes first, followed by preparing for re-use, recycling, other recovery such as energy recovery, and finally disposal, for example in landfill. Member States must apply the hierarchy as a priority order, but they may depart from it for specific waste streams where a life-cycle assessment shows that another option gives a better overall environmental outcome.

The directive and related laws contain binding targets for municipal waste, which covers mainly household waste and similar waste from businesses. At least 55% of municipal waste must be prepared for re-use or recycled by 2025, rising to 60% by 2030 and 65% by 2035. By 2035, no more than 10% may be landfilled. In 2023 the Commission warned several Member States that they risked missing the 2025 recycling target.

Separate collection has been extended over time. Since January 2025, Member States have had to collect textiles separately, and a revision of the directive adopted in 2025 requires them to set up extended producer responsibility schemes, under which producers of clothing and footwear pay for the collection and treatment of the textile waste they generate. The same revision sets targets for reducing food waste by 2030, in processing and manufacturing and in retail, restaurants and households.

Member States must always follow the waste hierarchy, whatever the waste stream or local conditions.
In the waste hierarchy, the only option ranked below energy recovery is disposal, for example in landfill.
Producer responsibility for textiles was introduced in order to fund the building of new recycling plants.

For passenger cars and vans, its limits on exhaust pollutants such as nitrogen oxides are largely the same as under the previous Euro 6 standard. New car types must comply from November 2026, and all newly registered cars a year later, with later deadlines for heavier vehicles.

Euro 7 tightens the exhaust limits for every category of road vehicle compared with Euro 6.
Brake particles are now a larger source of particulate pollution than exhaust from cars.
Carmakers used the savings from unchanged exhaust limits to expand electric car production.

Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere, yet plants cannot use it in its gaseous form. Before the twentieth century, farmers depended on manure, on rotating crops with legumes, whose root bacteria fix nitrogen, and on imported natural deposits such as Chilean saltpetre and guano. By the 1890s, scientists warned that these sources would not be enough to feed a growing world population.

In 1909 the German chemist Fritz Haber demonstrated in the laboratory that ammonia could be synthesised from nitrogen and hydrogen at high temperature and pressure, with the help of a catalyst. Carl Bosch, an engineer at the chemical company BASF, then turned the method into an industrial process, and the first plant began production in 1913. Both men later received Nobel Prizes in Chemistry. During the First World War, which broke out in 1914, the process was also used to supply nitrates for explosives, which helped Germany to continue fighting despite a naval blockade.

Today the Haber–Bosch process supplies most of the nitrogen in synthetic fertilisers. Some researchers estimate that around half of the world's population depends on food grown with it. It is, however, highly energy-intensive, and because the hydrogen is mostly produced from fossil fuels, chiefly natural gas, it is a significant source of carbon dioxide emissions.

options: Today the process supplies all of the nitrogen used in fertilisers around the world.
Without the process, around half of the world's population would now go hungry.
Haber received his Nobel Prize in Chemistry several years before Bosch received his.
The process was in industrial use before the outbreak of the First World War.

A solar cell converts light into electricity when photons free electrons in a semiconductor. Each semiconductor has a band gap, the minimum energy a photon must carry to free an electron. Photons with less energy than the band gap pass through without producing current, while photons with more energy produce current but lose the excess as heat. This trade-off sets a ceiling on efficiency.

In 1961 William Shockley and Hans-Joachim Queisser calculated this ceiling for a cell made of a single semiconductor under unconcentrated sunlight. The limit that bears their names is about 33% and is reached with a band gap of around 1.3 to 1.4 electronvolts. Silicon, which dominates the market, has a band gap of about 1.1 electronvolts; its own theoretical maximum, once other unavoidable losses are included, is usually put at around 29%. Good commercial silicon modules now convert more than 20% of sunlight into electricity.

The limit does not apply to cells that stack several materials with different band gaps, each capturing a different part of the solar spectrum. Such tandem cells, for example combining silicon with a perovskite layer, have exceeded 33% in the laboratory, although questions remain about how well perovskites withstand years of outdoor use.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Perovskite layers have been found unable to withstand years of outdoor use in tandem solar cells.
A cell that turns 36% of unconcentrated sunlight into electricity must combine more than one semiconductor.
Silicon dominates the market because it is cheaper to produce than other suitable semiconductors.
Shockley and Queisser predicted in 1961 that stacked cells would one day be able to exceed the limit they had calculated.

Over the past few million years, Earth's climate has swung repeatedly between glacial periods, when ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe, and warmer interglacials such as the present one. In the early twentieth century the Serbian engineer Milutin Milanković proposed that these cycles were paced by regular changes in Earth's orbit and axis.

Three changes matter most. The shape of the orbit varies from nearly circular to slightly elliptical over a cycle of roughly 100,000 years. The tilt of Earth's axis varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over around 41,000 years; a greater tilt makes summers warmer and winters colder in both hemispheres. Finally, the axis slowly wobbles, or precesses, which shifts the season in which Earth is closest to the Sun over a cycle of roughly 23,000 years. These changes alter the total sunlight Earth receives over a year very little, but they redistribute it between seasons and latitudes. What appears to matter most is summer sunshine at high northern latitudes, which decides whether winter snow survives to build ice sheets.

Milanković's theory gained wide acceptance after 1976, when analysis of deep-sea sediment cores revealed climate cycles matching his periods. Scientists stress, however, that orbital changes act as a pacemaker: feedbacks involving carbon dioxide and the reflectivity of ice amplify their effect.

options: A smaller axial tilt tends to cool far-northern summers, which in turn helps winter snow to persist there.
Changes in Earth's orbit and axis are enough on their own to explain the full scale of glacial cycles.
The present interglacial is expected to continue for tens of thousands of years, whatever humans do.
Scientists have established that northern summer sunshine is what determines the growth of ice sheets.

Grey wolves were eliminated from Yellowstone National Park in the United States by the 1920s, mainly through government predator-control programmes. In 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves captured in Canada were released in the park, and the population grew quickly. The reintroduction has since become one of the most cited examples of a trophic cascade, in which a top predator affects plants and landscapes indirectly through its effect on the animals it eats.

In the popular version of the story, wolves reduced the number of elk and also made them avoid risky places such as river banks. Willows and aspens, previously browsed heavily by elk, recovered; beavers returned; and stream banks stabilised. This 'landscape of fear' explanation spread widely through documentaries and online videos.

Many ecologists consider this account too simple. Elk numbers were also reduced by human hunting outside the park, by drought and by other predators such as bears and cougars, whose numbers rose during the same period. Some field studies tracking individual elk found little evidence that they avoided areas where wolves were most active. Some researchers argue that willows in places once heavily browsed have failed to recover because, with beavers long absent, streams have cut deeper channels and water tables have fallen. Most scientists agree that wolves have affected the park's ecosystem, but the strength of the effect remains disputed.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone in order to reduce the size of the elk herds that lived in the park.
Field studies have shown that elk never avoid the parts of the park where wolves are most active.
A fall in Yellowstone's elk population after 1995 would not by itself show that wolves were the cause.
Field studies have disproved the popular account of how wolves changed the park's landscape.

In the 1880s, two systems competed to supply electricity in the United States. Thomas Edison's companies promoted direct current (DC), which flows in one direction, while George Westinghouse, using patents licensed from Nikola Tesla, backed alternating current (AC), which reverses direction many times a second. The rivalry, later called the 'war of the currents', included public campaigns in which Edison's side stressed the dangers of high-voltage AC.

AC won mainly because of the transformer, which could raise its voltage for transmission and lower it again for safe use in homes. Transmitting power at high voltage reduces the current needed and therefore the energy lost as heat in the wires. With the technology of the time, DC voltage could not be changed easily, so DC systems needed power stations within a short distance of their customers.

The contest did not end the story of DC. Since the mid-twentieth century, high-voltage direct current (HVDC) links have been built where they perform better than AC, notably over very long distances and for undersea cables, in which AC suffers large losses. The converter stations at each end, which turn AC into DC and back, are expensive, so HVDC is generally chosen only when a link is long enough for its lower line losses to outweigh that cost.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Edison's campaign about the dangers of AC may have delayed its adoption in some American cities.
HVDC links have now replaced alternating current for long-distance power transmission across the world.
Tesla had worked for one of Edison's companies before his patents were licensed to Westinghouse.
All else being equal, sending power at a higher voltage lowers the energy wasted as heat in the lines.

In 1958 the American scientist Charles David Keeling began measuring the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air at an observatory on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii. The site was chosen because, at an altitude of over 3,000 metres and far from continents, the air there is well mixed and little affected by local sources such as cities or forests. The measurements, which continue today, produced the record now known as the Keeling Curve.

The first readings were around 315 parts per million (ppm). The concentration passed 400 ppm in 2013 and now exceeds 420 ppm, compared with about 280 ppm before the industrial revolution, a value known from air bubbles trapped in ice cores. The rise has not been steady: the annual increase in recent decades has been larger than in the 1960s.

Superimposed on the long-term rise is a seasonal cycle. The concentration falls during the northern growing season, from late spring to early autumn, as plants in the Northern Hemisphere take up carbon dioxide, and rises again in autumn and winter, when decomposition releases it. The Northern Hemisphere dominates the cycle because it contains much more land, and therefore much more vegetation, than the Southern Hemisphere. Measurements at other stations, including one at the South Pole, show a similar long-term rise but a much smaller seasonal swing.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The concentration of carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa has risen by the same amount every year since 1958.
In a given year, Mauna Loa readings are lower when the northern growing season ends than when it begins.
The size of the seasonal cycle at Mauna Loa has increased steadily since Keeling began his measurements in 1958.
Measurements at the South Pole show no seasonal variation in the concentration of carbon dioxide.

The European Pillar of Social Rights was proclaimed jointly by the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission at a summit in Gothenburg in November 2017. It sets out 20 principles grouped in three chapters: equal opportunities and access to the labour market, fair working conditions, and social protection and inclusion. The principles range from the right to education and training to the right to a minimum income, to affordable long-term care and to access to essential services such as water, energy and transport.

The proclamation itself does not create new legal obligations. Its principles are put into practice through a mix of EU legislation, funding and coordination of national policies, and many of the areas concerned remain largely the responsibility of Member States and of the social partners. In 2021 the Commission presented an action plan with three headline targets for the EU to reach by 2030: at least 78% of people aged 20 to 64 should be in employment, at least 60% of adults should take part in training every year, and the number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion should fall by at least 15 million, including at least 5 million children.

EU leaders welcomed these targets at a summit in Porto in May 2021, and Member States later set national targets of their own to contribute to them.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Pillar's 20 principles were proclaimed by EU leaders at the summit held in Porto in May 2021.
A legal right to a minimum income cannot be derived from the 2017 proclamation on its own.
The poverty target was introduced because the number of people at risk of poverty rose during the pandemic.
Under the 2030 targets, every adult in the EU is expected to take part in training each year.

The Directive on adequate minimum wages, adopted in 2022, had to be transposed by Member States by November 2024. It does not set a common minimum wage for the EU, nor does it oblige any country to introduce a statutory minimum wage. In most Member States a minimum wage is fixed by law, but in five of them, including Denmark, Sweden and Italy, minimum pay is determined through collective agreements, and these countries may keep that model.

For countries with a statutory minimum wage, the Directive requires clear procedures for setting and updating it. To assess whether it is adequate, they may use indicative reference values such as 60% of the gross median wage or 50% of the gross average wage. A separate provision applies to every Member State, whatever its wage-setting model: where fewer than 80% of workers are covered by collective agreements, the government must draw up an action plan to promote collective bargaining.

Denmark asked the Court of Justice to annul the Directive, arguing that the Treaties exclude pay from the EU's powers. In November 2025 the Court rejected most of the challenge. It annulled two specific provisions but left the rest of the Directive in force, including the rules on collective bargaining.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A country with no statutory minimum wage still needs an action plan if collective agreements cover only 70% of workers.
The Court annulled two of the provisions because they interfered too directly with the level of pay in Member States.
Each Member State must now set its minimum wage at no less than 60% of the gross median wage in that country.

The Pay Transparency Directive, adopted in 2023, aims to enforce the principle of equal pay for men and women for equal work or work of equal value. Member States had until June 2026 to bring it into national law. Several of its rights apply to all employers, whatever their size. Job applicants must be told the starting pay, or its range, for the post before the interview, for example in the vacancy notice, and employers may no longer ask candidates how much they earned in previous jobs. Workers may request information on their own pay level and on average pay levels, broken down by sex, for colleagues doing the same work or work of equal value. Contract terms that prevent workers from disclosing their pay in order to enforce equal pay are not allowed.

Reporting duties, by contrast, depend on size. Employers with at least 250 workers must report on their gender pay gap every year, those with 150 to 249 workers every three years, and those with 100 to 149 workers also every three years but only from a later date. Smaller employers have no such duty under the Directive, though Member States may impose one. Where reporting reveals a gap of at least 5% in any category of workers that the employer cannot justify on objective, gender-neutral grounds and does not correct within six months, a joint pay assessment must be carried out with workers' representatives.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Employers with 100 or more workers must report annually on the gender pay gap within their organisation.
Employers who ask job candidates about their previous salaries will face fines that are set at EU level.
A joint pay assessment is required wherever the overall gap between men's and women's pay exceeds 5%.
A firm with only 30 staff must still tell applicants the starting pay, or its range, before interviewing them.

The Work-Life Balance Directive, which Member States had to apply from August 2022, sets minimum standards for leave and flexible working for parents and carers. The right to the leave itself cannot depend on how long the worker has been employed, but Member States may make the payment conditional on up to six months of prior employment.

Each parent is also entitled to four months of parental leave, to be taken before the child reaches an age set by the Member State, of at most eight years. Two of these months cannot be transferred to the other parent and must be paid, at a level that each Member State defines. Workers who provide personal care or support to a relative, or to a person in the same household, who needs significant care for a serious medical reason are entitled to five working days of carers' leave per year. The Directive leaves it to Member States to decide whether this leave is paid.

Parents of children up to at least eight years old and carers may also request flexible arrangements, such as reduced hours or remote work. Employers must respond within a reasonable period and give reasons for any refusal.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?

Carers' leave is usually paid at the level of national sick pay, in the same way as paternity leave.
A father employed for three months before the birth is entitled to paternity leave, though it may be unpaid.

The Platform Work Directive, adopted in 2024, is the first piece of EU law to regulate the use of algorithms in managing people at work. Member States have until December 2026 to transpose it. In 2021 the Commission estimated that more than 28 million people in the EU worked through digital labour platforms, in activities ranging from ride-hailing and food delivery to translation and data entry, and that many of them may have been wrongly classified as self-employed.

To address misclassification, the Directive introduces a legal presumption of employment. Where facts indicating control and direction are found, as determined under national law and collective agreements and taking into account the case law of the Court of Justice, the person is presumed to be in an employment relationship with the platform. The presumption can be rebutted, but it is then for the platform to prove that the relationship is not one of employment. The Directive does not itself list the criteria for triggering the presumption, nor does it automatically reclassify anyone.

On algorithmic management, platforms may not use automated systems to process data on a person's emotional or psychological state or on private conversations. Decisions that significantly affect a person, such as suspending an account, must be taken by a human being. These protections apply to everyone working through a platform, including those who are genuinely self-employed.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Once facts triggering the national-law presumption of employment are found, a courier need not prove an employment relationship herself.
Most of the 28 million platform workers counted by the Commission were engaged in ride-hailing or food delivery.
From December 2026, everyone who works through a digital labour platform will be treated as an employee.

In 1935 the American psychologist John Ridley Stroop published a study that became one of the most frequently replicated findings in experimental psychology. He asked participants to name the colour of the ink in which words were printed. When the words were names of colours printed in a different colour, such as the word 'red' printed in blue ink, people took considerably longer to name the ink colour than when they named the colours of plain coloured squares. Reading the words aloud, by contrast, was hardly slowed by a mismatched ink colour.

The standard explanation is that, for literate adults, reading is a highly practised and largely automatic process, whereas naming colours requires more deliberate attention. When the two conflict, the automatic response has to be suppressed, which takes time and sometimes fails, producing errors. Consistent with this account, extended practice at naming colours tends to reduce the interference without removing it.

The task is now widely used to study attention and self-control, and versions of it appear in clinical research. Researchers caution, however, that the size of the effect varies with factors such as practice, the language of the words and the exact design of the task, so a single score says little about an individual.

During an outbreak in Soho in 1854, Snow mapped the homes of those who died and found that they clustered around a public water pump in Broad Street. Some apparent exceptions supported his case: workers at a nearby brewery, who were given beer and had their own well, were largely spared, while some victims living further away turned out to have preferred the Broad Street water. On his advice the local authorities removed the pump handle. The number of new cases had, however, already been falling before the handle was removed, partly because many residents had fled the area, so the episode alone did not prove his theory.

Stronger evidence came from Snow's comparison of households in south London supplied by two water companies, one drawing its water from a stretch of the Thames contaminated by sewage and the other from further upstream. The idea that the language people speak shapes the way they think is often called the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis, after the linguist Edward Sapir and his student Benjamin Lee Whorf, although neither formulated it as a single testable hypothesis. In its strong form, known as linguistic determinism, it holds that language sets the limits of thought, so that speakers cannot form concepts for which their language has no words. Most linguists and psychologists now reject this version: people can perceive and reason about distinctions their language does not mark, and new words are coined readily when they are needed.

A weaker claim, that language influences certain kinds of thinking, has found some experimental support. Russian, for example, has separate basic terms for lighter and darker blues. In one study, Russian speakers told two shades of blue apart more quickly when they fell on different sides of the Russian boundary than when they fell on the same side, while English speakers showed no such difference. The advantage disappeared when the Russian speakers had to perform a verbal task at the same time, suggesting that language was involved at the moment of judgement.

Even supporters of the weaker claim stress that such effects are usually small and depend on the task. Critics add that findings from one pair of languages cannot simply be generalised to others.

In 1786 William Jones, a British judge in India, observed that Sanskrit bore so strong a resemblance to Greek and Latin, in verb roots and grammatical forms, that the three must have sprung from a common source which perhaps no longer existed. He was not the first to notice such similarities, but his remark is often taken as the starting point of comparative linguistics. The family descended from that source is now known as Indo-European. It includes most languages of Europe, among them the Germanic, Romance, Slavic and Celtic languages, as well as Persian and many languages of northern India.

Linguists reconstruct the lost parent language, Proto-Indo-European, by comparing words in its descendants and working out the regular sound correspondences between them. Latin pater, Greek patēr and Sanskrit pitar, for example, correspond to English father, reflecting a systematic change by which an original p became f in the Germanic languages. Similarities that do not follow regular correspondences are treated with suspicion, because they may result from borrowing or chance.

No texts in Proto-Indo-European survive, so reconstructed forms are hypotheses and are marked with an asterisk. Several languages spoken in Europe, including Basque, Finnish, Estonian and Hungarian, do not belong to the family.

The demographic transition model describes how populations change as societies develop. In the first stage, both birth and death rates are high and the population grows slowly, if at all. In the second, death rates fall, thanks mainly to a better food supply, sanitation and medicine, while birth rates remain high, so the population grows rapidly. In the third stage birth rates also decline, as more children survive, education spreads and families choose to have fewer children, and growth slows. In the fourth, both rates are low and the population is roughly stable.

The model was developed from the experience of Western Europe, where the transition took well over a century, and it describes rather than explains: it does not specify why fertility starts to fall when it does, and the timing has varied considerably between countries. Many countries in Asia and Latin America passed through the stages much faster than Europe did.

Some demographers add a fifth stage for countries where fertility has fallen well below the replacement level, which in countries with low mortality is about 2.1 children per woman: the level at which a population replaces itself in the long run without migration. In such countries deaths may eventually exceed births, and the population may decline unless immigration makes up the difference.

The Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe was signed in Rome in October 2004. It was intended to replace the existing treaties with a single text, to give the Union a single legal personality and to make the Charter of Fundamental Rights legally binding. Like other treaties amending the founding treaties, it had to be ratified by every Member State, either by a parliamentary vote or, where national rules or political choices required it, by a referendum.

The early results were encouraging for its supporters. Spanish voters approved it in February 2005 by a large majority, although fewer than half of those entitled to vote took part. Then, within a week, the treaty was rejected in France on 29 May 2005 by about 55% of voters and in the Netherlands on 1 June by about 62%, on turnouts considerably higher than in Spain. Analyses of the French vote suggested that many voters were motivated by domestic concerns such as unemployment, as well as by objections to the text itself.

Luxembourg nevertheless approved the treaty in a referendum in July 2005, but several governments postponed their planned votes, and the European Council called for a 'period of reflection'. The constitutional project was eventually abandoned, although much of its institutional content was later carried over into a conventional amending treaty.

The European Chips Act entered into force in September 2023. Its headline aim is to double the EU's share of global semiconductor production capacity, from around 10% to 20% by 2030, in a market that is itself expected to grow strongly. The Act has three strands. The first, the Chips for Europe Initiative, supports research, pilot lines and design capacity, bridging the gap between laboratory and factory. The second sets a framework for 'first-of-a-kind' production facilities, which can benefit from faster permitting and, within EU state aid rules, from public support granted by Member States. The third creates a mechanism to monitor supply chains and respond to shortages, coordinated by a European Semiconductor Board.

The Commission has said the Act should mobilise more than €43 billion of public and private investment. Most of that sum, however, is expected to come from Member States and industry rather than from the EU budget.

Critics argue that the target is unrealistic. In a report published in 2025, the European Court of Auditors concluded that the 20% goal was unlikely to be reached, and some large factory projects announced in recent years have since been delayed or cancelled. Supporters reply that the Act was also meant to strengthen resilience and monitoring, not merely to reach a single market-share figure.

The NIS2 Directive, which replaced the EU's first directive on network and information security, had to be transposed into national law by October 2024. Many Member States missed that deadline, and the Commission opened infringement procedures against most of them. The directive widens the range of sectors covered, from energy, transport, banking and health to waste management, food production, space and parts of the digital economy, and divides the organisations concerned into 'essential' and 'important' entities.

As a rule, NIS2 applies to medium-sized and large organisations in the listed sectors, and small companies fall outside it. There are exceptions, however: some providers, such as top-level domain name registries and providers of public electronic communications networks, are covered whatever their size. Covered entities must take appropriate measures to manage cybersecurity risks, and their management bodies must approve those measures and can be held responsible for failures to comply.

Reporting is staged. A significant incident must be notified to the competent authority or to the national computer security incident response team: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, a fuller notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month. Member States must provide for maximum fines of at least €10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for essential entities, and €7 million or 1.4% for important entities.

The Cyber Resilience Act, which entered into force in December 2024, sets cybersecurity requirements for 'products with digital elements': hardware and software that can connect, directly or indirectly, to another device or to a network. It covers items as varied as smart toys, home routers, operating systems and password managers. Products already regulated by sector-specific rules with comparable requirements, such as medical devices and motor vehicles, are excluded, and so is free and open-source software that is not supplied in the course of a commercial activity.

The Act applies in stages. Manufacturers' duty to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, both to a designated national computer security incident response team and to ENISA, the EU cybersecurity agency, applies from September 2026, whereas most other obligations apply from December 2027. Manufacturers must design products to be secure and handle vulnerabilities throughout a support period that reflects how long the product is expected to be in use, normally at least five years, providing security updates during that time.

For most products, manufacturers may assess their own compliance before affixing the CE marking. Certain categories listed as 'important' or 'critical', such as firewalls, face stricter procedures, which may require an assessment by an independent body.

Under the revised EU regulation on electronic identification, which entered into force in May 2024, every Member State must offer its citizens and residents at least one European Digital Identity Wallet by the end of 2026. The wallet is an application, typically on a smartphone, that lets users identify themselves online and in person, store digital documents such as a driving licence or a university diploma, and sign documents electronically.

The wallet must be free of charge for individuals, and its use is voluntary: people who choose not to use it must not be disadvantaged when they access public or private services. A central design principle is selective disclosure. A user should be able to prove a single attribute, for instance that they are over 18, without revealing other data such as their full date of birth or their address. Wallet providers may not collect information about how the wallet is used beyond what is needed to provide the service.

Acceptance is being phased in. Public services that require electronic identification must accept the wallet, and so, when users ask to use it, must very large online platforms and private services that are legally required to authenticate users strongly, such as banks. Member States are building their wallets on common technical specifications, so that a wallet issued in one country can be used across the Union.

The Data Act, which has applied since September 2025, sets rules on who may access and use the data generated by connected products, such as cars, smart household appliances and industrial machinery, and by related services. Users of such products, whether consumers or businesses, are entitled to access the data their use generates and may ask for it to be shared with a third party of their choice, for example an independent repair service. Connected products placed on the market after September 2026 must be designed so that, where technically feasible, this data is directly accessible to users by default.

The right has limits. Trade secrets remain protected, and a data holder may refuse to share them where disclosure would very probably cause it serious economic damage, provided it can justify that decision. Companies designated as gatekeepers under the EU's digital competition rules are not eligible to receive data as third parties under this right.

The Act also aims to make it easier to switch between cloud providers. Providers must remove obstacles to switching, and charges for switching are being phased out: until January 2027 they may not exceed the costs directly linked to the switch, and from then on they are not allowed at all. Finally, public bodies may request data from companies in situations of exceptional need, such as a public emergency.

The European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, known as EuroHPC, was set up in 2018 and is based in Luxembourg. It pools resources from the EU, participating countries and private partners to acquire and operate world-class supercomputers, which are hosted by national computing centres across Europe. Its systems include LUMI in Kajaani, Finland, Leonardo in Bologna, Italy, and MareNostrum 5 in Barcelona, Spain. JUPITER, installed at Jülich in Germany, was designed as Europe's first exascale machine, able to perform a billion billion calculations per second, and a second exascale system is planned in France.

Computing time on these machines is allocated mainly through calls for proposals assessed on scientific merit, and access for research is generally free of charge for users based in the EU and in participating countries. Scientists use the machines for climate modelling, drug discovery, materials science and other demanding tasks.

In 2024 the joint undertaking's mandate was extended to artificial intelligence. It now supports 'AI Factories', which give start-ups, researchers and industry access to computing resources suited to training large AI models, and it has also begun to acquire quantum computers to be integrated with its supercomputers. Energy use is a recurring concern: LUMI, for example, runs on hydroelectric power, and the waste heat it produces helps to warm homes in the surrounding area.

In the early twentieth century, Henrietta Swan Leavitt, working at the Harvard College Observatory, studied large numbers of variable stars on photographic plates of the Small Magellanic Cloud. Among them was a class now called Cepheid variables, which brighten and dim in a regular cycle. In 1912 she reported that the brighter Cepheids had longer periods. Because the stars in the Cloud are all at roughly the same distance from Earth, differences in their apparent brightness had to reflect real differences in the light they emit.

This period–luminosity relation made Cepheids usable as 'standard candles'. By timing a Cepheid's cycle, astronomers could infer how much light it actually gives off; comparing that with how bright it appears then reveals its distance. At first, however, Leavitt's relation gave only relative distances, and it had to be calibrated using nearby Cepheids whose distances could be measured independently.

In the 1920s Edwin Hubble identified Cepheids in what was then called the Andromeda Nebula and showed that it lay far beyond the Milky Way, settling a long debate about whether such spiral nebulae were separate galaxies. Later work revealed that there are two types of Cepheids, each with its own relation, and correcting the earlier confusion between them roughly doubled the estimated distances to other galaxies in the 1950s.

The first planet found orbiting a Sun-like star was announced in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, who later shared a Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery. Planets had been detected three years earlier around a pulsar, the collapsed remnant of a massive star, but 51 Pegasi b was the first found around an ordinary star like the Sun. It was detected with the radial velocity method: as a planet orbits, it tugs its star slightly back and forth, and the wavelength of the star's light shifts accordingly. This method gives a lower limit for the planet's mass.

Most of the more than 6,000 exoplanets confirmed since then have been found with the transit method, which watches for the slight, regular dimming that occurs when a planet passes in front of its star. A transit reveals the planet's size relative to the star, but it can be seen only if the orbit is aligned almost edge-on from our point of view, so many planetary systems can never be detected in this way.

Both methods find large planets on close orbits more easily than small, distant ones, because these produce stronger and more frequent signals. When a planet is detected by both methods, astronomers can combine its mass and size to estimate its density, and hence whether it is more likely to be rocky or gaseous.
