Radiocarbon dating, developed by the American chemist Willard Libby in the late 1940s, earned him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960. It relies on carbon-14, a radioactive form of carbon produced in the upper atmosphere through the action of cosmic rays on nitrogen. Plants absorb carbon-14 along with ordinary carbon through photosynthesis, and animals take it in by eating plants, so living organisms keep roughly the same proportion of carbon-14 as their surroundings. When an organism dies it stops taking in carbon, and the carbon-14 it contains decays at a known rate, halving about every 5,730 years. Measuring how much remains therefore indicates how long ago death occurred.

The method can be applied only to material that once contained carbon from living things, such as wood, bone, charcoal or textiles. After about 50,000 years so little carbon-14 is left that it can no longer be measured reliably. Moreover, the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere has varied over time, so raw results must be calibrated against records of known age, such as tree rings.

Modern accelerator mass spectrometry counts carbon-14 atoms directly and needs only milligrams of material, compared with the grams required by earlier techniques. This has made it possible to date precious objects while causing only minimal damage.

Anchoring is the tendency for an initial number to pull later estimates towards it, even when that number is plainly irrelevant. In a well-known experiment reported in 1974, the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a wheel of fortune, rigged to stop at either 10 or 65, in front of participants. They then asked them whether the percentage of African countries in the United Nations was higher or lower than the number on the wheel, and finally to estimate the actual percentage. Participants who had seen 10 gave a median estimate of 25%; those who had seen 65 gave a median estimate of 45%.

Later studies have found anchoring effects among experienced professionals as well as students. In one study, estate agents' valuations of a house were influenced by the asking price they were shown, although most of them said the price had played no part in their judgement. Anchors appear to work partly by making information consistent with the anchor easier to call to mind.

Simply warning people about the bias does little to reduce it. A strategy that has shown some success is to 'consider the opposite', deliberately listing reasons why the anchor might be inappropriate, although this weakens the effect rather than eliminating it.

Regression to the mean is a statistical phenomenon first described by Francis Galton in the 1880s. Studying the heights of parents and their adult children, he found that very tall parents tended to have children who were tall, but on average less extreme than themselves, while very short parents tended to have children who were short but closer to the average. Galton initially read this as a biological tendency towards mediocrity, but the effect is statistical. It arises whenever two measurements are imperfectly correlated, because an extreme result usually owes something to chance factors that are unlikely to recur.

The phenomenon often misleads people who evaluate interventions. Daniel Kahneman described flight instructors who believed that praise harmed performance and criticism improved it, since a trainee praised after an excellent landing usually did worse the next time, while one criticised after a poor landing usually did better. Both patterns would be expected even if feedback had no effect at all.

The same trap arises in public policy. Road junctions are often selected for speed cameras after an unusually bad year for accidents. A fall in accidents the following year is then partly to be expected anyway, so a credible evaluation must compare the treated junctions with similar sites that received no camera, or use data covering a longer period.

Most of a human cell's DNA is packed into the nucleus, but mitochondria, the structures that supply cells with energy, carry a small genome of their own. In humans it is a circular molecule of roughly 16,600 base pairs containing 37 genes, compared with about three billion base pairs in the nuclear genome. A cell may contain hundreds or thousands of copies of mitochondrial DNA but only two copies of the nuclear genome.

Mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost exclusively from the mother, because the father's mitochondria are normally eliminated after fertilisation; only a handful of cases of paternal transmission have been reported. It therefore passes down the female line largely unchanged, apart from occasional mutations, and is not reshuffled in each generation as nuclear DNA is.

These properties make it valuable to forensic scientists and archaeologists. Because there are so many copies, it can often be recovered from old or degraded samples when nuclear DNA cannot. A skeleton found under a car park in Leicester in 2012 was later identified as that of King Richard III, in part by comparing its mitochondrial DNA with that of living descendants of his eldest sister through an unbroken female line. Mitochondrial DNA cannot, however, distinguish between people who share the same maternal ancestry, such as siblings.

The identification of Richard III's skeleton also relied on radiocarbon dating of the bones.

In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once formed a single landmass and had since drifted apart. He set out his case in a book first published in 1915. His evidence was varied: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle; similar fossils of land animals and plants occur on continents now separated by oceans; rock formations match across the Atlantic; and traces of ancient glaciers appear in regions that are now tropical.

Most geologists rejected the idea for decades. Their main objection was not to the evidence of past connections, which some explained by land bridges that had since sunk, but to the lack of a plausible mechanism: Wegener could not explain convincingly what force could move continents through the solid ocean floor, and the forces he suggested were shown to be far too weak. Wegener died on an expedition to Greenland in 1930, with his theory still widely dismissed.

The picture changed in the 1950s and 1960s, when surveys of the ocean floor revealed mid-ocean ridges and symmetrical bands of magnetised rock on either side of them. These findings showed that new crust forms at the ridges and spreads outwards, which supplied the kind of mechanism that had been missing. By the end of the 1960s, plate tectonics, which incorporated continental drift, had become the accepted framework of geology.

Wegener's book was widely translated and was read by many geologists outside Germany.

In 1966 the psychologist Peter Wason devised a simple-looking test of logical reasoning. Participants see four cards, each with a letter on one side and a number on the other, showing for example E, K, 4 and 7. They are told a rule: 'If a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side.' Their task is to turn over those cards, and no others, that are needed to find out whether the rule has been broken.

The correct answer is E and 7. The E card must be checked because an odd number on its back would break the rule, and so must the 7, because a vowel on its back would also break it. The 4 is irrelevant: the rule says nothing about what must lie behind an even number. In many studies, fewer than one participant in ten has chosen correctly; the most common answers are E alone, or E and 4.

Performance changes dramatically when the same logical structure is presented as a familiar social rule. If participants imagine checking that 'anyone drinking beer must be over 18', most correctly decide to check the beer drinker and the person under 18, not the cola drinker or the adult. Researchers still disagree about why. Some argue that people have a specialised ability to detect cheaters; others stress familiarity with rules about permission and obligation.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: In every study of the abstract version, fewer than one participant in ten has managed to choose correctly.
Researchers now agree that people do better on the drinking version because they are good at spotting cheaters.

A participant who turned over E, 4 and 7 would have turned over one more card than the task required.
